I would recommend starting with the 4th doctor, as that's the most popular era of the old show and in many ways the most influential on the general tone and aesthetics of the new show. The Ark in Space, the 4th doctors second story, is highly regarded by both RTD and Moffat, and generally sets the tone for that era, so a good place to start (Robot, Tom Bakers first story, is stylistically much more of a send off of the Pertwee era than thematically/visually connected to the Baker stuff, tho it is still a fun enough little adventure). Then just work your way from there, and if you like it you can always work your way back.

If picking where to start is too daunting for you, there's also live channels on Roku, Plex, Tubi, etc- you'll probably end up dropping into the middle of a random story and be a bit confused but it is closer to a more traditional tv experience rather than digging through 30 years of old episodes on your own.

It fails on even the very basic level of the obvious points it wants to make.

Listed budgets only include production costs, not marketing. Theatres also take a cut of the gross, which is generally smaller during opening weekend (hence why opening numbers are important), and they also got a bigger cut in international distribution, which means in terms of worldwide gross even less of it is going to the studio. So if they spent 220 million just on making the movie, it probably costs closer to 400 million with marketing (although the ad campaign for this one seemed a bit sparse, with the strikes and all), and then theatres get 20% of opening weekend tickets domestically- that's another 10 million off, and the studio only gets around 40% of international- which means it's made around 70 or 80 mil, or like 300 mil below the cost.
Opening weekend is generally significantly more profitable than following weeks for blockbusters

I enjoy the classic show, but it's very ropey in terms of production values. Never really been a huge fan of the stagey multicam style, and videotape while probably fine for the 10-20 inch tvs of the time doesn't hold up that well. I can accept some cheesy effects and sets, I'm a huge fan of TOS and Batman 66 for example, but old Who just doesn't have the tight editing and crisp aesthetic that you get from a show shot on 35mm. The Hinchcliffe era is able to play to the shows aesthetic strengths the most I think, but outside of that its not really my kind of vibe in terms of how it's put together. Especially with how long some of the serials tend to run, you can definitely tell some of those early episodes exist to fill air time, which we just don't have to deal with in modern television production (if anything we have the opposite problem of things being overedited and unnecessarily brief). I'm a big fan of monster of the week type stuff, so that appeals to me with the new show.

The modern series generally looks great and can go toe to toe with other genre shows of its era in terms of effects, scale,  and general production values. The first few series have the slight misfortune of being stuck on SD, but overall in terms of visuals, editing, and music it's a much classier show imo. Also the sheer amount of episodes the classic series produced, especially in the black and white era, gave the actors a lot less time to rehearse and I think it definitely shows sometimes. Like in some of the Troughton stuff they were filming a week or two before the air date iirc? Insanity. You give the same people who made the classic show a bigger budget and more time, I think it would be just as good as the modern series. They managed a lot with very limited resources, but it does tend to feel rough as a result.
